title: Heat Pump vs Oil, Propane and Baseboard Heat

scenes.purpose: Name the three heating fuels the video is about.

visual.description: Warm field; "Propane, oil, baseboards" settles in large type, each word lighting as it is spoken.

scenes.narration: If your house runs on propane, heating oil or electric baseboards, someone has probably told you a heat pump is the easy win.

scenes.purpose: Pose the question the video answers.

visual.description: The question types on, centred; "always" turns amber as it is spoken.
onScreenText: Does a heat pump always beat each of them?

scenes.narration: But does a heat pump always beat each of them on running cost, or does one of them break the rule?

scenes.purpose: Give the confident claim in the marketplace's own words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "almost everywhere" turns green as it is spoken.
onScreenText: "Heat pumps consistently save against propane, oil, and electric resistance heating almost everywhere."

scenes.narration: The home-energy marketplace EnergySage puts it flatly: "Heat pumps consistently save against propane, oil, and electric resistance heating almost everywhere."

scenes.purpose: Give the same claim for oil, from a video.

visual.description: Quote card, text only, mirrored from the previous one; "always" turns green as it is spoken.
onScreenText: "always also going to be more expensive than a heat pump"

scenes.direction: Wipe from the previous quote card.
scenes.narration: Abode Energy Management, in a video on heat pump economics in Massachusetts, says home heating oil is "always also going to be more expensive than a heat pump".

scenes.purpose: Give the counter-report that breaks the rule for oil.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "increase by a few hundred dollars" turns red as it is spoken.
onScreenText: "could see their energy costs increase by a few hundred dollars over the cold season"

scenes.direction: Wipe in; hold after the last word before the investigation.
scenes.narration: Yet The Boston Globe reported that in a winter of cheaper oil, even Massachusetts homeowners switching from oil "could see their energy costs increase by a few hundred dollars over the cold season".

scenes.purpose: Turn from claims to evidence, starting wide.

visual.description: "The widest view" in large type, the camera pulling back as it lands.

scenes.narration: So who is right? Start with the widest view.

scenes.purpose: Show the national estimate for oil, propane and electric homes that already have air conditioning.

visual.description: Two tiles: share of homes with lower bills on s07, median yearly saving on s08.

chart.title: Homes on electricity, oil or propane, with air conditioning
chart.note: Modelled estimate across heat pump efficiency levels, not measured bills.

scenes.direction: First tile on s07, second on s08.
scenes.narration: A national study estimated that among homes heating mainly with electricity, fuel oil or propane that already have air conditioning, 95 to 100 percent would see lower bills with a heat pump, depending on its efficiency. The median saving it estimated was $300 to $650 a year.

scenes.purpose: Show the same fuels doing worse without air conditioning.

visual.description: One tile, amber against the previous green: the share with lower bills drops.

chart.title: Same fuels, without air conditioning
chart.note: Most homes whose bills rose were in hotter climates, where new cooling cost more than the heating saved.

scenes.narration: Homes on those fuels without air conditioning did worse: only 73 to 86 percent would come out ahead, and most of the homes whose bills went up were in hotter climates, where the new cooling cost more than the heating saved.

scenes.purpose: Set gas-heated homes beside them for comparison.

visual.description: Two tiles: the median loss in red, the median saving in green.

chart.title: Gas-heated homes with air conditioning, median per year
chart.note: The first tile is a loss, not a saving.

scenes.direction: Loss tile on "loss", saving tile on "saving"; hold a beat.
scenes.narration: For comparison, among gas-heated homes with air conditioning, the same study put the median anywhere from a $70 loss to a $380 saving, depending on the heat pump.

scenes.purpose: Turn from estimates to measurements.

visual.description: The question types on; "real homes" lights as it is spoken.
onScreenText: What about heat pumps running in real homes?

scenes.narration: That was an estimate. What about heat pumps running in real homes?

scenes.purpose: Give the measured saving against electric resistance heat.

visual.description: One large tile, 53%, counting up as the figure is spoken.

chart.title: Cold-climate heat pumps, all-electric systems

points.label: Average heating cost cut vs electric resistance

chart.note: The baseline is electric resistance meeting the same load, not oil or propane.

citations.label: CEE 2018, cold-climate heat pump field study

scenes.narration: A study of cold-climate heat pumps found the all-electric systems cut heating costs by 53 percent on average, measured against what electric resistance heaters would have used for the same heat.

scenes.purpose: Show the evaluation's finding against resistance and propane in its own words.

visual.description: The evaluation's paragraph; the highlight sweeps across the mini-split result as it is spoken.

excerpt.highlight: DMSHPs proved more cost-effective for all energy prices

scenes.narration: An evaluation of ductless mini-split heat pumps found them more cost-effective than electric resistance and propane heat at every energy price and every outdoor temperature it examined.

scenes.purpose: Show the oil exception in the same paragraph.

visual.description: Same paragraph; the highlight moves down to the oil sentence, in amber.

excerpt.highlight: For oil-fired systems, the relative energy price determines the

scenes.narration: Oil was different: there, the relative price of oil decided the outdoor temperature above which the heat pump won.

scenes.purpose: Give the switch-off temperatures, tied to each year's prices.

visual.description: Two lines build: "Below 8°F in 2015" then "Below 25°F in 2016", each as its figure is spoken, in icy blue.

scenes.direction: Each line on its figure; hold after the sentence.
scenes.narration: So the evaluators advised oil-heated homes to switch the heat pump off when it got very cold, when the oil system would run cheaper: below 8 degrees Fahrenheit in one year, and below 25 degrees the next, depending on that year's energy prices.

scenes.purpose: Show the broader study's finding that savings are higher off gas.

visual.description: The study's paragraph; the highlight marks the net-benefit clause, then the caveat line lights faintly.

excerpt.highlight: expensive and thus the net benefits of heat pumps are higher

citations.label: Edwards et al. 2024, heat pump bill savings

scenes.narration: And another study found that in regions where homes heat with electricity or fuels other than gas, heating is generally more expensive and the net benefits of a heat pump are higher, though climate and energy prices also play an important role.

scenes.purpose: Show real projects splitting both ways.

visual.description: Two tiles: the number of projects, then the largest yearly cost increase, in red.

chart.title: Home electrification projects with cost data
chart.note: Some projects raised costs; the big reductions were most likely in homes heating with propane or fuel oil.

citations.label: Less et al. 2021, LBNL retrofit costs

scenes.narration: Real projects show the same split: across 273 home electrification projects with cost data, some raised annual energy costs, in some cases by as much as $1,000 a year, while the big reductions were most likely in homes with high bills beforehand, such as those heating with propane or fuel oil.

scenes.purpose: Return to the question before the answer.

visual.description: The question types on again, as in the opening.
onScreenText: So does a heat pump always win?

scenes.direction: Hold a beat before the answer.
scenes.narration: So does a heat pump always win?

scenes.purpose: Give the answer fuel by fuel.

visual.description: Two lines build one per sentence: the propane and resistance line in green, the oil line in amber.
onScreenText: Propane and electric resistance: nearly always
Oil: depends on the price and the cold

scenes.direction: Line one on s25, line two on s26.
scenes.narration: Against propane and electric resistance heat, this evidence says it nearly always does on running cost. Against oil, not always: whether it wins depends on the price of oil and how cold it gets.

scenes.purpose: Name what the evidence cannot settle for one house.

visual.description: Three words stack as they are spoken: air conditioning, climate, energy prices.

citations.label: Wilson et al. 2024; Edwards et al. 2024

scenes.narration: What none of this can do is price your own house: the results moved with air conditioning, climate and energy prices.

scenes.purpose: Advice for propane and baseboard homes.

visual.description: "Get installed quotes" in large type.

scenes.narration: If you heat with propane or baseboards, get installed quotes and set them against what you spend on fuel each winter.

scenes.purpose: Advice for oil homes: the switchover question.

visual.description: The question types on; "outdoor temperature" in icy blue.
onScreenText: Below what outdoor temperature does your old system run cheaper?

scenes.narration: If you heat with oil, ask a different question: at this winter's oil and electricity prices, below what outdoor temperature does your old system run cheaper, and will you keep it for those days?

scenes.purpose: Close on the one action.

visual.description: "Check your fuel and your rates" settles in large type; fade out.
onScreenText: Check your fuel and your rates

scenes.direction: Fade to black after the last word.
scenes.narration: Check your fuel and your rates before you check the brochure.
